newsitem.title: FRANCE: France is major loser in Zaire revolt.
newsitem.headline: France is major loser in Zaire revolt.

text.p: The battle for control of Zaire is not yet over but one loser is already clear -- France.

By supporting discredited President Mobutu Sese Seko to the last and trying in vain to mobilise the international community to intervene, Paris has isolated itself and alienated the Tutsi rebels who have overrun much of eastern Zaire as the ragged army has looted and fled.
The relentless advance of the rebels led by Laurent Kabila amid ineffectual appeals from Paris has highlighted a decline in French power in central Africa, where it once called the shots.
While Mobutu, 66, languishes with prostate cancer in a Monaco hospital, support for him seems to crumble daily in Kinshasa and French policy seems to have lost its way.

"We are not seeking to gain anything of any kind in this part of Africa," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Monday, trying to distance France from the debacle after the rebels captured Zaire's third-largest city, Kisangani.
"Frankly, I do not believe that we have any real interests in this part of the world. We have duties, but that is true also for the entire international community," he said.

Diplomats say the French have no major economic interests in Zaire, a mineral-rich former Belgian colony reduced to virtual bankruptcy after 32 years of autocratic Mobutu rule, but they do have strategic interests in the region.
"Their real interest in the stability of Zaire is ensuring there is no spillover into Angola, Gabon and Congo where they have substantial oil interests," one European envoy said.

Another said Zaire was such a vast land-mass -- Africa's third largest state -- that Paris could not be indifferent to who controls the country, and especially the capital, Kinshasa, which has five million residents, including a sizeable French expatriate community.
A French policymaker confirmed that contagion was the Paris government's biggest fear.
"Anyone who thinks a Liberia-style civil war in a country on the scale of Zaire would stop conveniently at the borders is living in a dream-world," he said.

While acknowledging Mobutu's faults, French officials say the rebellion was instigated and aided by English-speaking Uganda and its Tutsi allies in Rwanda and Burundi, with the tacit encouragement of the United States.

Washington sought to allay such suspicions on Monday, saying it was troubled by reports that the rebels were receiving help and guns from the governments of Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and Angola and adding that Zaire's territorial integrity "is terribly important for stability throughout Central Africa".

U.S. officials say Mobutu was useful to the West as a rampart against Soviet influence in African from the 1960s until the late 1980s, but since the end of the Cold War, he had become a liability, immune to economic or political reform.
France has tried recently to promote a transition to democratic rule in Zaire, hoping that elections would provide a scenario for an orderly transfer of power.
But it has continued to assign a key role to Mobutu, who aborted the last attempt at democratisation launched in 1990 and has consistently avoided ceding real power to any elected body.
De Charette insisted only this month that the president, once described by a French minister as "a walking safe with a leopard-skin hat", remained indispensible to any transition.
One insider said France had completely neglected Kabila, seeing the rebel leader as a mere pawn in the hands of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni.

Experts trace the French loss of influence in central Africa to the 1994 civil war in Rwanda, when French-backed Hutu forces massacred hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tutsis before the Ugandan-backed Tutsi-led Rwandan Popular Front took power.

More than a million Hutu refugees fled to Zaire, where France sought Mobutu's blessing to stage a military operation to provide them with humanitarian assistance. In return, Mobutu emerged from quarantine, was invited to a Franco-African summit and allowed to visit his French Riviera villa regularly.
In the eyes of many Tutsis, the French protected Hutu militiamen guilty of genocide from being brought to justice.

"France took the wrong positions, notably on the Rwandan genocide, and the Americans took advantage of that," said Jean-Pierre Chretien, an Africa expert at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS).

"If France does not change policy very fast in Africa, then the future history of Africa will be written against France," said Francois-Xavier Verschave, president of the African development association "Survie" (survival).
